To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the primary but not secondary scales of the PDQ-4 were retrieved in a general population of 774 men and 742 women; and (2) the primary scales are reliable and valid measures of their hypothesized dimensions.

1) the personality deviance scales were retrieved in a 2 factor analysis of a large general population of older men and women; 2) the personality deviant scales are reliable and stable; 3) the scales are correlated with measures of personality and mental health and with measures of life adjustment and well-being; 4) the scales are sensitive to changes in mental health; 5) the scales can differentiate between groups known to differ in personality deviance; and, 6)
the primary but (not) the secondary scales of PDS were retrieved in the factor analysis of the data from the general population of older adult men and women.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new personality inventory that will measure personality deviance, that is, the degree to which an individual's personality is at odds with his or her culture's norms.
the study of the personality structure of the older adult.
the development of a measure of personality deviance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the primary but no the secondary scales of this instrument are appropriate for use with older adults of the general population.
the primary scales, as a group, were found to be more reliable than the secondary scales.
there are no significant differences in mean scores for the primary scales between the general population and a group of older adults.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the primary but neither the secondary nor the tertiary scales are useful for the assessment of personality deviance in a general population sample of older adults.
the personality deviance concept is not only useful for the study of psychopathology but is also applicable in normal populations.
the primary scales of the Personality Disorder Inventory (PDI) were found to be reliable, valid and useful in the assessment of personality disorders in older adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
personality deviance scales may be useful in the assessment of older adults in clinical settings, but that they may be less useful in research.
the primary scales of the Personality Disorder Inventory (PDI) are not a good measure of PDs.
the primary scales of the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5; Personality Inventory for the DSM-5) are more likely to be useful in older adult samples than the secondary scales.
